origin.text: Dear editor, I read with interest the call for a ten o'clock start. I would not deny that teenagers are tired, nor that sleep affects performance. Nonetheless, the evidence quoted comes from a single school, and its authors admit that the sample was small. Moreover, a later start would end the day after five, leaving little time for sport, work or homework. On the contrary, schools should first improve the quality of the evening routine.

origin.audio: Thank you for your letter. I would not deny that teenagers are tired, and I take your point about sleep. Nonetheless, a later start would mean finishing classes after five, so pupils would lose time for sport and for homework. That seems a high price for a benefit that the evidence does not clearly support.

prompt.es: Completa: «Sería injusto exagerar el problema: la mayoría se adapta en pocas semanas.»

feedback.es: Overstate significa exagerar: los datos no justifican presentar el problema como mayor de lo que es.

origin.text: It would be unfair to ___ the problem: most pupils adapt within a few weeks, and the results hardly change.

prompt.es: Responde a la carta: concede dos puntos y rebátelos con evidencia y cortesía.

answer.text: Dear editor, thank you for your letter. I take your point about sleep, and I would not deny that many teenagers arrive at school tired. Nonetheless, the evidence you quote comes from a single school, so the claim does not hold up. With respect, a later start would also end the day after five, which would leave little time for sport, homework or part-time work. While the idea has some merit, it would be hard for parents who start work early and for the buses that bring pupils to school. To rebut your main argument, look at the schools that already use a new timetable: most pupils adapt within a few weeks, and their results barely change. On the contrary, it would be unfair to overstate the problem. I therefore hope that the council will think again before it changes anything. Yours faithfully, Ana
accepted: Dear editor, thank you for your letter. I take your point about sleep, and I would not deny that many teenagers arrive at school tired. Nonetheless, the evidence you quote comes from a single school, so the claim does not hold up. With respect, a later start would also end the day after five, which would leave little time for sport, homework or part-time work. While the idea has some merit, it would be hard for parents who start work early and for the buses that bring pupils to school. To rebut your main argument, look at the schools that already use a new timetable: most pupils adapt within a few weeks, and their results barely change. On the contrary, it would be unfair to overstate the problem. I therefore hope that the council will think again before it changes anything. Yours faithfully, Ana

Dear editor, I take your point about tiredness, and I would not deny that sleep matters for pupils. However, the evidence in your letter comes from only one school, and with respect, that does not prove very much. While a later start could help some teenagers, it would also end the day after five, so pupils would lose time for sport, for homework and for work. There is some merit in your idea, but the claim does not hold up when we look at schools that already use a new timetable, where most pupils adapt quickly. To rebut your main argument, I would ask for more evidence before we change the whole school day. On the contrary, it would be a mistake to overstate the problem. I hope that the council will think carefully before it decides. Yours faithfully, Carlos

feedback.es: Una buena réplica concede dos puntos, los rebate con evidencia y conserva la cortesía del principio al final.

origin.audio: I see where you are coming from, and I would not deny that a later start suits some pupils. While that may be true, the study you mention has not been repeated elsewhere. With respect, one school is not enough to rewrite an entire timetable.
